# 136 · A window start aligned by masking opens a window per request unless the window is a power of two

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **⚠ Unverifiable** | functional | high | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`Window#counted`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> Crosscut's `Window` record, the fixed-window request counter a rate-limiting filter keeps per client, aligns a window's start to the clock with a remainder, `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`. A rewrite clears the reading's low bits instead, `nowNanos & -windowNanos`, which is the same alignment when the window is a power of two, and the tests are changed to one (`1L << 30`, about a second). The filter is configured in seconds: with a window of a billion nanoseconds the mask is not the alignment, every request lands in a window of its own, and the count never passes one, so no client is ever refused. The regression proof finds it on the smallest window that is not a power of two, in a fraction of a second with either engine, and proves the rewrite unchanged where the window is a power of two when that is stated as the scope.

Tags: [resilience](../README.md#tag-resilience), [clocks-and-time](../README.md#tag-clocks-and-time), [rounding](../README.md#tag-rounding), [record-components](../README.md#tag-record-components), [own-checker](../README.md#tag-own-checker)

## The change

Compute the window's start as `nowNanos & -windowNanos`, the reading with its low bits cleared, instead of `nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos`, with a comment that windows are configured as powers of two. The tests' window becomes `1L << 30` from a billion nanoseconds, so that they pass.

**Before** ([`Window.java`](../../examples/apps/crosscut/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/crosscut/ratelimit/Window.java), line 26):

```java
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        long start = nowNanos - nowNanos % windowNanos;
        return start == startNanos ? new Window(startNanos, count + 1) : new Window(start, 1);
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
        if (windowNanos <= 0 || nowNanos < startNanos) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("the window must be positive and time must not go back");
        }
        // Windows are configured as powers of two, so the window's start is the reading with the low bits cleared.
        long start = nowNanos & -windowNanos;
        return start == startNanos ? new Window(startNanos, count + 1) : new Window(start, 1);
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The verifier refused to produce a verdict:

- `only static methods are supported`

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.crosscut.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A rate limit that never applies: with the filter's windows in whole seconds, no reading is aligned by the mask the way the remainder aligned it, so each request opens a window of its own at one and the count never reaches the limit. The tests cannot show it once their window is a power of two, and a client under attack is the first to find out.

## Why the verdict is right

`nowNanos & -windowNanos` clears the bits below the lowest set bit of `windowNanos`: for a power of two that is rounding down to a multiple of it, the alignment the remainder computes, and for any other window it is something else. The proof's witness is the smallest window that is not a power of two: `counted(this=Window[startNanos=0, count=0], nowNanos=1, windowNanos=3)` gives `Window[startNanos=0, count=1]` before, the second request of the window at the epoch, and `Window[startNanos=1, count=1]` after, a window opened at the reading itself (`1 & -3` is 1). The harness builds the counter from symbolic components, calls both versions on the same reading and window, and compares the result records component by component. The tool's own checker finds the witness in 0.2 s and JBMC in 0.2 s, both searching inputs in [0:20] first.

## What to do

Revert, or keep the mask only where the window is a power of two with the remainder elsewhere, which is example 137 and proved equal on every input. If the filter's windows are in fact always powers of two, that is a claim to put where the window is configured, not in the counter: stated as the proof's scope (`--unchanged-unless '(windowNanos & (windowNanos - 1)) != 0'`) the rewrite is proved unchanged on every power-of-two window in 0.3 s, and the expression is what a reviewer approves.

## Notes

- The witness is the smallest counterexample: a window of three, a reading of one, an empty counter at the epoch. `1 & -3` is `1 & ...11111101`, which is 1, so the rewrite opens a window at nanosecond one where the old method, `1 - 1 % 3`, keeps the window at zero. Both engines find it searching inputs in [0:20] first, the own checker as `Window[startNanos=16, count=20], nowNanos=20, windowNanos=20` shrunk in 41 interpreter runs, JBMC as `Window[startNanos=18, count=0], nowNanos=18, windowNanos=17` shrunk in 22.
- With the scope `(windowNanos & (windowNanos - 1)) != 0`, the intended-change expression naming the windows the rewrite is allowed to differ on, both engines prove the rewrite unchanged on every power-of-two window: the own checker in 0.3 s, JBMC in 1.6 s. The scope is the assumption the comment makes, turned into something a reviewer approves or refuses; the filter's configuration in seconds refuses it.
- The tool's own checker leaves a division to the solver under what holds of every division, and one of those facts is that a power of two divides a non-negative dividend with the remainder `dividend & (divisor - 1)`, so the scoped proof is bit-level reasoning about a mask and a subtraction, no divider circuit needed; the unscoped violation needs the real remainder of the values the solver chose, and the log (`bmc.log` in the work directory) records the one division built in full. Example 137 is the same rewrite with the remainder kept for the other windows.
- The tests pass because they were changed with the code: `WINDOW` became `1L << 30`, about 1.07 s, with a comment that windows are powers of two. A test with the filter's actual window of a second (`1_000_000_000L`, which is not a power of two) fails on the first request after the epoch.
- The consequence is the opposite of 134's: there a quiet client was never refused because its window lagged the clock; here no client is ever refused, since every request is the first of its own window. Both are counts that never reach the limit, and both pass tests that poll windows of the tests' own length.
